  "passage_text": "SECTION CCXCI

"'Yudhishthira said, "O thou of mighty arms, tell me, after this what is
beneficial for us. O grandsire, I am never satiated with thy words which
seem to me like Amrita. What are those good acts, O best of men, by
accomplishing which a man succeeds in obtaining what is for his highest
benefit both here and hereafter, O giver of boons!"

"'Bhishma said, "In this connection I shall narrate to thee what the
celebrated king Janaka had enquired, in days of yore, of the high-souled
Parasara, 'What is beneficial for all creatures both in this world and
the next! Do thou tell me what should be known by all this connection.'
Thus questioned, Parasara, possessed of great ascetic merit and
conversant with the ordinances of every religion,[1497] said these words,
desirous of favouring the king.

"'"Parasara said, 'Righteousness earned by acts is supreme benefit both in
this world and the next. The sages of the old have said that there is
nothing higher than Righteousness. By accomplishing the duties of
righteousness a man becomes honoured in heaven. The Righteousness, again,
of embodied creatures, O best of kings, consists in the ordinance (laid
down in the scriptures) on the subject of acts.[1498] All good men
belonging to the several modes of life, establishing their faith on that
righteousness, accomplish their respective duties.[1499] Four methods of
living, O child, have been ordained in this world. (Those four methods
are the acceptance of gifts for Brahmanas; the realisation of taxes for
Kshatriyas; agriculture for Vaisyas; and service of the three other
classes for the Sudras). Wherever men live the means of support come to
them of themselves. Accomplishing by various ways acts that are virtuous
or sinful (for the purpose of earning their means of support), living
creatures, when dissolved into their constituent elements attain to
diverse ends.[1500] As vessels of white brass, when steeped in liquefied
gold or silver, catch the hue of these metals, even so a living creature,
who is completely dependent upon the acts of his past lives takes his
colour from the character of those acts. Nothing can sprout forth without
a seed. No one can obtain happiness without having accomplished acts
capable of leading to happiness. When one's body is dissolved away (into
its constituent elements), one succeeds in attaining to happiness only in
consequence of the good acts of previous lives. The sceptic argues, O
child, saying, I do not behold that anything in this world is the result
of destiny or the virtuous and sinful acts of past lives. Inference
cannot establish the existence or operation of destiny.[1501] The
deities, the Gandharvas and the Danavas have become what they are in
consequence of their own nature (and not of their acts of past lives).
People never recollect in their next lives the acts done by them in
previous ones. For explaining the acquisition of fruits in any particular
life people seldom name the four kinds of acts alleged to have been
accomplished in past lives.[1502] The declarations having the Vedas for
their authority have been made for regulating the conduct of men in this
world, and for tranquillizing the minds of men. These (the sceptic says),
O child, cannot represent the utterances of men possessed of true wisdom.
This opinion is wrong. In reality, one obtains the fruits of whatever
among the four kinds of acts one does with the eye, the mind, the tongue,
and muscles.[1503] As the fruit of his acts, O king, a person sometimes
obtains happiness wholly, sometimes misery in the same way, and sometimes
happiness and misery blended together. Whether righteous or sinful, acts
are never destroyed (except by enjoyment or endurance of their
fruits).[1504] Sometimes, O child, the happiness due to good acts remains
concealed and covered in such a way that it does not display itself in
the case of the person who is sinking in life's ocean till his sorrows
disappear. After sorrow has been exhausted (by endurance), one begins to
enjoy (the fruits of) one's good acts. And know, O king, that upon the
exhaustion of the fruits of good acts, those of sinful acts begin to
manifest themselves. Self-restraint, forgiveness, patience, energy,
contentment, truthfulness of speech, modesty, abstention from injury,
freedom from the evil practices called vyasana, and cleverness,--these
are productive of happiness. No creature is eternally subject to the
fruits of his good or bad acts. The man possessed of wisdom should always
strive to collect and fix his mind. One never has to enjoy or endure the
good and bad acts of another. Indeed, one enjoys and endures the fruits
of only those acts that one does oneself. The person that casts off both
happiness and misery walks along a particular path (the path, viz., of
knowledge). Those men, however, O king, who suffer themselves to be
attached to all worldly objects, tread along a path that is entirely
different. A person should not himself do that act which, if done by
another, would call down his censure. Indeed, by doing an act that one
censures in others, one incurs ridicule. A Kshatriya bereft of courage, a
Brahmana that takes every kind of food, a Vaisya unendued with exertion
(in respect of agriculture and other moneymaking pursuits), a Sudra that
is idle (and, therefore, averse to labour), a learned person without good
behaviour, one of high birth but destitute of righteous conduct, a
Brahmana fallen away from truth, a woman that is unchaste and wicked, a
Yogin endued with attachments, one that cooks food for one's own self, an
ignorant person employed in making a discourse, a kingdom without a king
and a king that cherishes no affection for his subjects and who is
destitute of Yoga,--these all, O king, are deserving of pity!'"'"[1505]"
}

  "passage_text": "SECTION CCXCII\n\n\"'\"Parasara said, 'That man who, having obtained this car, viz., his body\nendued with mind, goes on, curbing with the reins of knowledge the steeds\nrepresented by the objects of the senses, should certainly be regarded as\npossessed of intelligence. The homage (in the form of devotion to and\nconcentrated meditation on the Supreme) by a person whose mind is\ndependent on itself and who has cast off the means of livelihood is\nworthy of high praise,--that homage, namely, O regenerate one, which is\nthe result of instructions received from one who has succeeded in\ntranscending acts but not obtained from the mutual discussion of men in\nthe same state of progress.[1506] Having obtained the allotted period of\nlife, O king, with such difficulty, one should not diminish it (by\nindulgence of the senses). On the other hand, man should always exert, by\nrighteous acts for his gradual advancement.[1507] Among the six different\ncolours that Jiva attains at different periods of his existence, he who\nfalls away from a superior colour deserves obloquy and censure. Hence,\none that has attained to the result of good acts should conduct oneself\nin such a way as to avoid all acts stained by the quality of Rajas.[1508]\nMan attains to a superior colour by righteous acts. Unable to acquire a\nsuperior hue, for such acquisition is extremely difficult, a person, by\ndoing sinful acts only slays himself (by sinking into hell and falling\ndown into an inferior colour). All sinful acts that are committed\nunconsciously or in ignorance are destroyed by penances. A sinful act,\nhowever, that is committed knowingly, produces much sorrow. Hence, one\nshould never commit sinful acts which have for their fruit only sorrow.\nThe man of intelligence would never do an act that is sinful in character\neven if it leads to the greatest advantage, just as a person that is pure\nwould never touch a Chandala.[1509] How miserable is the fruit I see of\nsinful acts! Through sin the very vision of the sinner becomes perverse,\nand he confounds his body and its unstable accompaniments with the\nSoul.[1510] That foolish man who does not succeed in betaking himself to\nRenunciation in this world becomes afflicted with great grief when he\ndeparts to the next world.[1511] An uncoloured cloth, when dirty, can be\ncleaned, but not a piece of cloth that is dyed with black; even so, O\nking, listen to me with care, is it the case with sin. That man who,\nhaving knowingly committed sin, acts righteously for expiating that sin,\nhas to enjoy and endure the fruits of his good and bad acts\nseparately.[1512] The utterers of Brahma maintain, under the authority of\nwhat has been laid down in the Vedas, that all acts of injury committed\nin ignorance are cancelled by acts of righteousness. A sin, however, that\nis committed consciously is never cancelled by righteousness. Thus say\nthe regenerate utterers of Brahma who are conversant with the scriptures\nof Brahmana. As regards myself, my view is that whatever acts are done,\nbe they righteous or sinful, be they done knowingly or otherwise, remain\n(and are never destroyed unless their fruits are enjoyed or\nendured).[1513] Whatever acts are done by the mind with full\ndeliberation, produce, according to their grossness or subtility, fruits\nthat are gross or subtile.[1514] Those acts, however, O thou of righteous\nsoul, which are fraught with great injury, if done in ignorance, do\nwithout fail produce consequences and even consequences that lead to\nhell, with this difference that those consequences are disproportionate\nin point of gravity to the acts that produce them.[1515] As to those acts\n(of a doubtful or unrighteous nature) that may be done by the deities or\nascetics of reputation, a righteous man should never do their like or,\ninformed of them, should never censure them.[1516] That man who,\nreflecting with his mind, O king, and ascertaining his own ability,\naccomplishes righteous acts, certainly obtains what is for his benefit.\nWater poured into an unbaked vessel gradually becomes less and finally\nescapes altogether. If kept, however, in a baked vessel, it remains\nwithout its quantity being diminished. After the same manner, acts done\nwithout reflection with the aid of the understanding do not become\nbeneficial; while acts done with judgment remain with undiminished\nexcellence and yield happiness as their result. If into a vessel\ncontaining water other water be poured, the water that was originally\nthere increases in quantity; even so all acts done with judgment, be they\nequitable or otherwise, only add to one's stock of righteousness. A king\nshould subjugate his foes and all who seek to assert their superiority,\nand he should properly rule and protect his subjects. One should ignite\none's sacred fires and pour libations on them in diverse sacrifices, and\nretiring in the woods into either one's middle or old age, should live\nthere (practising the duties of the two last modes of life). Endued with\nself-restraint, and possessed of righteous behaviour, one should look\nupon all creatures as on one's own self. One should again reverence one's\nsuperiors. By the practice of truth and of good conduct, O king, one is\nsure to obtain happiness.'\"'\""
}

  "passage_text": "SECTION CCXCIII\n\n\"'\"Parasara said, 'Nobody in this world does good to another. Nobody is\nseen to make gifts to others. All persons are seen to act for their own\nselves. People are seen to cast off their very parents and their uterine\nbrothers when these cease to be affectionate. What need be said then of\nrelatives of other degrees?[1517] Gifts to a distinguished person and\nacceptance of the gifts made by a distinguished person both lead to equal\nmerit. Of these two acts, however, the making of a gift is superior to\nthe acceptance of a gift.[1518] That wealth which is acquired by proper\nmeans and increased also by proper means, should be protected with care\nfor the sake of acquiring virtue. This is an accepted truth. One desirous\nof acquiring righteousness should never earn wealth by means involving\ninjury to others. One should accomplish one's acts according to one's\npower, without zealously pursuing wealth. By giving water, whether cold\nor heated by fire, with a devoted mind, unto a (thirsty) guest, according\nto the best of one's power, one earns the merit that attaches to the act\nof giving food to a hungry man. The high-souled Rantideva obtained\nsuccess in all the worlds by worshipping the ascetics with offerings of\nonly roots and fruits and leaves. The royal son of Sivi also won the\nhighest regions of felicity by having gratified Surya along with his\ncompanion with offerings of the same kind. All men, by taking birth, incur\ndebts to gods, guests, servants, Pitris, and their own selves. Everyone\nshould, therefore, do his best for freeing himself from those debts. One\nfrees oneself from one's debt to the great Rishis by studying the Vedas.\nOne pays off one's debts to the gods by performing sacrifices. By\nperforming the rites of the Sraddha one is freed from one's debts to the\nPitris. One pays off one's debt to one's fellowmen by doing good offices to\nthem. One pays off the debts one owes to one's own self by listening to\nVedic recitations and reflecting on their import, by eating the remnants of\nsacrifices, and by supporting one's body. One should duly discharge all\nthe acts, from the beginning, that one owes to one's servants. Though\ndestitute of wealth, men are seen to attain to success by great\nexertions.[1519] Munis by duly adoring the deities and by duly pouring\nlibations of clarified butter on the sacred fire, have been seen to\nattain to ascetic success. Richika's son became the son of Vishwamitra.\nBy adoring the deities who have shares in sacrificial offerings, with\nRichs (he attained to success in after life). Usanas became Sukra by\nhaving gratified the god of gods. Indeed, by hymning the praises of the\ngoddess (Uma), he sports in the firmament, endued with great\nsplendour.[1520] Then, again, Asita and Devala, and Narada and Parvata,\nand Karkshivat, and Jamadagni's son Rama, and Tandya possessed of\ncleansed soul, and Vasishtha, and Jamadagni, and Viswamitra and Atri, and\nBharadwaja, and Harismasru, and Kundadhara, and Srutasravas,--these great\nRishis, by adoring Vishnu with concentrated minds with the aid of Richs,\nand by penances, succeeded in attaining to success through the grace of\nthat great deity endued with intelligence. Many undeserving men, by\nadoring that good deity, obtained great distinction. One should not seek\nfor advancement by achieving any wicked or censurable act. That wealth\nwhich is earned by righteous ways is true wealth. Fie on that wealth,\nhowever, which is earned by unrighteous means. Righteousness is eternal.\nIt should never, in this world, be abandoned from desire of wealth. That\nrighteous-souled person who keeps his sacred fire and offers his daily\nadorations to the deities is regarded as the foremost of righteous\npersons. All the Vedas, O foremost of kings, are established on the three\nsacred fires (called Dakshina, Garhapatya, and Ahavaniya). That Brahmana\nis said to possess the sacred fire whose acts exist in their entirety. It\nis better to at once abandon the sacred fire than to keep it, abstaining\nthe while from acts. The sacred fire, the mother, the father who has\nbegotten, and the preceptor, O tiger among men, should all be duly waited\nupon and served with humility. That man who, casting off all feelings of\npride, humbly waits upon and serves them that are venerable for age, who\nis possessed of learning and destitute of lust, who looketh upon all\ncreatures with an eye of love, who has no wealth, who is righteous in his\nacts, and who is destitute of the desire of inflicting any kind of harm\n(upon any one), that truly respectable man is worshipped in this world by\nthose that are good and pious.'\"'\"[1521]"

Such service, rendered with\naffection and reverence, makes them righteous.[1522] If the ancestors of\nany Sudra were not engaged in service, he should not still engage himself\nin any other occupation (than service). Truly, he should apply himself to\nservice as his occupation. In my opinion, it is proper for them to\nassociate, under all circumstances, with good men devoted to\nrighteousness, but never with those that are wicked. As regards the Sudras,\nthey should engage themselves in the task of humbly and honestly\ncollecting together the articles that are to be offered in sacrifices,\nand in cleaning altars and other places where sacrifices are to be\nperformed. Keeping aside gifts\nby thousands, even twenty cowries that one may give painfully, having\nearned them righteously, will be productive of the great benefit. The Brahmana shines by self\nrestraint; the Kshatriya by victory; the Vaisya by wealth; while the\nSudra always shines in glory through cleverness in serving (the three\nother orders).'\"'\""

Sudra that earned by serving the three other orders, however small its
measure, is worthy of praise, and spent for the acquisition of virtue is

servitor of the three other classes. If the Brahmana, pressed for a
living, betakes himself to the duties of either the Kshatriya or the
Vaisya, he does not fall off from righteousness. When, however, the
Brahmana betakes himself to the duties of the lowest order, then does he
certainly fall off. When the Sudra is unable to obtain his living by
service of the three other orders, then trade, rearing of cattle, and the
practice of the mechanical arts are lawful for him to follow. Appearance
on the boards of a theatre and disguising oneself in various forms,
exhibition of puppets, the sale of spirits and meat, and trading in iron
and leather, should never be taken up for purposes of a living by one who
had never before been engaged in those professions every one of which is
regarded as censurable in the world. It hath been heard by us that if one
engaged in them can abandon them, one then acquires great merit. When one
that has become successful in life behaves sinfully in consequence of
one's mind being filled with arrogance, one's acts under such
circumstances can never pass for authority. It is heard in the Puranas
that formerly mankind were self-restrained; that they held righteousness
in great esteem; that the practices they followed for livelihood were all
consistent with propriety and the injunctions laid down in the
scriptures, and that the only punishment that was required for chastising
them when they went wrong was the crying of fie on them.[1525] At the
time of which we speak, O king, Righteousness, and nothing else, was much
applauded among men. Having achieved great progress in righteousness, men
in those days worshipped only all good qualities that they saw. The
Asuras, however, O child, could not bear that righteousness which
prevailed in the world. Multiplying (in both number and energy), the
Asuras (in the form of Lust and Wrath) entered the bodies of men. Then
was pride generated in men that is so destructive of righteousness. From
pride arose arrogance, and from arrogance arose wrath. When men thus
became overwhelmed with wrath, conduct implying modesty and shame
disappeared from them, and then they were overcome by heedlessness.
Afflicted by heedlessness, they could no longer see as before, and as the
consequence thereof they began to oppress one another and thereby acquire
wealth without any compunction. When men became such, the punishment of
only crying fie on offenders failed to be of any effect. Men, showing no
reverence for either the gods or Brahmanas, began to indulge their senses
to their fill.[1526] At that time the deities repaired to that foremost
of gods, viz., Siva, possessed of patience, of multiform aspect, and
endued with the foremost of attributes, and sought his protection. The
deities imparted unto him their conjoined energy, and thereupon the great
god, with a single shaft, felled on the earth those three Asuras, viz.,
Desire, Wrath, and Cupidity, who were staying in the firmament, along
with their very habitations.[1527] The fierce chief of those Asuras
possessed of fierce prowess, who had struck the Devas with terror, was
also slain by Mahadeva armed with the lance.[1528] When this chief of the
Asuras was slain, men once more obtained their proper natures, and once
more began to study the Vedas and the other scriptures as was in former
times. Then the seven ancient Rishis came forward and installed Vasava as
the chief of the gods and the ruler of heaven. And they took upon
themselves the task of holding the rod of chastisement over mankind.
After the seven Rishis came king Viprithu (to rule mankind), and many
other kings, all belonging to the Kshatriya order for separately ruling
separate groups of human beings. (When Mahadeva dispelled all evil
passions from the minds of creatures) there were, in those ancient times,
certain elderly men from whose minds all wicked feelings did not fly
away. Hence, in consequence of that wicked state of their minds and of
those incidents that were connected with it, there appeared many kings of
terrible prowess who began to indulge in only such acts as were fit for
Asuras. Those human beings that are exceedingly foolish adhere to those
wicked acts, establish them as authorities, and follow them in practice
to this day.[1529] For this reason, O king, I say unto thee, having
reflected properly with the aid of the scriptures, that one should
abstain from all acts that are fraught with injury or malice and seek to
acquire a knowledge of the Soul.[1530] The man possessed of wisdom would
not seek wealth for the performance of religious rites by ways that are
unrighteous and that involve an abandonment of morality. Wealth earned by
such means can never prove beneficial. Do thou then become a Kshatriya of
this kind. Do thou restrain thy senses, be agreeable to thy friends, and
cherish, according to the duties of thy order, thy subjects, servants,
and children. Through the union of both prosperity and adversity (in
man's life), there arise friendships and animosities. Thousands and
thousands of existences are continually revolving (in respect of every

to faults. Such is the character of good qualities that if the most
foolish person, bereft of every virtue, hears himself praised for any
good quality, he becomes filled with joy. Virtue and sin exist, O king,
only among men. These do not exist among creatures other than man. One"

"'"Janaka said, 'Whence, O great Rishi, does this difference of colour
arise among men belonging to the different orders? I desire to know this.
Tell me this, O foremost of speakers! The Srutis say that the offspring
one begets are one's own self. Originally sprung from Brahmana, all the
inhabitants of the earth should have been Brahmanas. Sprung from
Brahmanas, why have men betaken themselves to practices distinguished
from those of Brahmanas.'

"'"Parasara said, 'It is as thou sayst, O king! The offspring procreated
are none else than the procreator himself. In consequence, however, of
falling away from penance, this distribution into classes of different
colours has taken place. When the soil becomes good and the seed also is
good, the offspring produced become meritorious. If, however, the soil
and seed become otherwise or inferior, the offspring that will be born
will be inferior. They that are conversant with the scriptures know that
when the Lord of all creatures set himself to create the worlds, some
creatures sprang from his mouth, some from his arms, some from his
thighs, and some from his feet. They that thus sprang from his mouth, O
child, came to be called Brahmanas. They that sprang from his arms were
named Kshatriyas. They, O king, that sprang from his thighs were the
wealthy class called the Vaisyas. And, lastly, they that were born of his
feet were the serving class, viz., the Sudras. Only these four orders of
men, O monarch, were thus created. They that belong to classes over and
other than these are said to have sprung from an intermixture of these.
The Kshatriyas called Atirathas, Amvashthas, Ugras, Vaidehas, Swapakas,
Pukkasas, Tenas, Nishadas, Sutas, Magadhas, Ayogas, Karanas, Vratyas, and
Chandalas, O monarch, have all sprung from the four original orders by
intermixture with one another.'

"'"Janaka said, 'When all have sprung from Brahmana alone, how came human
beings to have diversity in respect of race? O best of ascetics, an
infinite diversity of races is seen in this world. How could men devoted
to penances attain to the status of Brahmanas, though of indiscriminate
origin? Indeed, those born of pure wombs and those of impure, all became
Brahmanas.'

"'"Parasara said, 'O king, the status of high-souled persons that succeeded
in cleansing their souls by penances could not be regarded as affected by
their low births. Great Rishis, O monarch, by begetting children in
indiscriminate wombs, conferred upon them the status of Rishis by means
of their power of asceticism. My grandfather Vasishtha, Rishyasringa,
Kasyapa, Veda, Tandya, Kripa, Kakshivat, Kamatha, and others, and
Yavakrita, O king, and Drona, that foremost of speakers, and Ayu, and
Matanga, and Datta, and Drupada, and Matsya, all these, O ruler of the
Videhas, obtained their respective positions through penance as the
means. Originally only four Gotras (races) arose, O monarch, viz.,
Angiras, Kasyapa, Vasishtha, and Bhrigu. In consequence of acts and
behaviour, O ruler of men, many other Gotras came into existence in time.
The names of those Gotras have been due to the penances of those that
have founded them. Good people use them.'

"'"Janaka said, 'Tell me, O holy one, the especial duties of the several
orders. Tell me also what their common duties are. Thou art conversant
with everything.'

"'"Parasara said, 'Acceptance of gifts, officiation at the sacrifices of
others, and the teaching of pupils, O king, are the especial duties of
the Brahmanas. The protection of the other orders is proper for the
Kshatriya. Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the occupations of
the Vaisyas. While service of the (three) regenerate classes is the
occupation, O king, of the Sudras. I have now told thee what the especial
duties are of the four orders, O monarch. Listen now to me, O child, as I
tell thee what the common duties are of all the four orders. Compassion,
abstention from injury, heedfulness, giving to others what is due to
them, Sraddhas in honour of deceased ancestors, hospitality to guests,
truthfulness, subjugation of wrath, contentedness with one's own wedded
wives, purity (both internal and external), freedom from malice,
knowledge of Self, and Renunciation,--these duties, O king, are common to
all the orders. Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and Vaisyas,--these are the three
regenerate orders. All of them have an equal right to the performance of
these duties, O foremost of men. These three orders, betaking themselves
to duties other than those laid down for them, come to grief, O monarch
(and fall down from their own status), even as they go up and acquire
great merit by taking for their model some righteous individual of their
respective classes who is duly observant of his own duties. The Sudra
never falls down (by doing forbidden acts); nor is he worthy of any of
the rites of regeneration. The course of duties flowing from the Vedas is
not his. He is not interdicted, however, from practising the three and
ten duties that are common to all the orders. O ruler of the Videhas,
Brahmanas learned in the Vedas, O monarch, regard a (virtuous) Sudra as
equal to Brahmana himself. I, however, O king, look upon such a Sudra as
the effulgent Vishnu of the universe, the foremost one in all the
worlds.[1544] Persons of the lowest order, desiring to exterminate the
evil passions (of lust and wrath, etc.) may betake themselves to the
observance of the conduct of the good; and, indeed, while so acting, they
may earn great merit by performing all rites that lead to advancement,
omitting the mantras that are utterable by the other orders while
performing the self-same ceremonies. Wherever persons of the lowest order
adopt the behaviour of the good, they succeed in attaining to happiness
in consequence of which they are able to pass their time in felicity both
here and hereafter.'"

of the preceptors of men that are destitute of devotion are unable to

firmly devoted to such seniors, that speak what is agreeable to them,
that seek their welfare, and that are submissive to them in behaviour,
can obtain the merit of devotion. The sire is the highest of deities with
his children. It is said that the sire is superior to the mother. The
attainment of Knowledge is regarded as the highest acquisition. They that
have subjugated the objects of the senses (by attainment of Knowledge),
acquire what is highest (viz., Emancipation). That Kshatriya prince who,

one that has been disarmed, or one that is weeping, or one that is
unwilling to fight, or one that is unequipped with mail and cars and
horse and infantry, or one that has ceased to exert oneself in the fight,
or one that is ill, or one that cries for quarter, or one that is of
tender years, or one that is old. A Kshatriya should, in battle, fight
one of his order who is equipped with mail and cars and horse and
infantry, who is ready for exertion and who occupies a position of
equality. Death at the hands of one that is equal or of a superior is
laudable, but not that at the hands of one that is low, or of one that is
a coward, or of one that is a wretch. This is well-known. Death at the
hands of one that is sinful, or of one that is of low birth and wicked
conduct, O king, is inglorious and leads to hell. One whose period of
life has run out cannot be rescued by anybody. Similarly, one whose
period of life has not been exhausted can never be slain by any
one.[1547] One should prevent one's affectionate seniors from doing unto
one (for one's benefit) such acts as are done by menials, as also all
such acts as are fraught with injury to others. One should never desire
to extend one's own life by taking the lives of others.[1548] When they
lay down their lives, it is laudable for all householders observant of
the duties of men living in sacred places to lay down their lives on the
banks of sacred streams.[1549] When one's period of life becomes
exhausted, one dissolves away into the five elements. Sometimes this
occurs suddenly (through accidents) and sometimes it is brought about by
(natural) causes.[1550] He who, having obtained a body, brings about its
dissolution (in a sacred place by means of some inglorious accident),
becomes invested with another body of a similar kind. Though set on the
path of the Emancipation, he yet becomes a traveller and attains to
another body like a person repairing from one room into another.[1551] In
the matter of such a man's attainment of a second body (notwithstanding
his death in a sacred spot) the only cause is his accidental death. There
is no second cause. That new body which embodied creatures obtain (in
consequence of the accidental character of their deaths in sacred places)
comes into existence and becomes attached to Rudras and Pisachas.[1552]

conglomeration of arteries and sinews and bones and much repulsive and
impure matter and a compound of (primal) essences, and the senses and
objects of the senses born of desire, all having an outer cover of skin
close to them. Destitute (in reality) of beauty and other
accomplishments, this conglomeration, through force of the desires of a
previous life, assumes a human form.[1553] Abandoned by the owner, the
body becomes inanimate and motionless. Indeed, when the primal
ingredients return to their respective natures, the body mingles with the
dust. Caused by its union with acts, this body reappears under
circumstances determined by its acts. Indeed, O ruler of the Videhas,
under whatever circumstances this body meets with dissolution, its next
birth, determined by those circumstances, is seen to enjoy and endure the
fruits of all its past acts. Jiva, after dissolution of the body it
inhabited, does not, O king, take birth in a different body immediately.
It roves through the sky for some time like a spacious cloud. Obtaining a
new receptacle, O monarch, it then takes birth again. The soul is above
the mind. The mind is above the senses. Mobile creatures, again, are
foremost of all created objects. Of all mobile creatures those that have
two legs are superior. Amongst two-legged creatures, those that are
regenerate are superior. Amongst those that are regenerate they that are
possessed of wisdom are superior. Amongst them that are possessed of
wisdom they that have succeeded in acquiring a knowledge of the soul are
superior. Amongst those that are possessed of a knowledge of the soul,
they that are endued with humility are superior. Death follows birth in
respect of all men. This is settled. Creatures, influenced by the
attributes of Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas, pursue acts which have an
end.[1554] That man is regarded as righteous who meets with dissolution
when the Sun is in the northern declension, and at a time and under a
constellation both of which are sacred and auspicious. He is righteous
who, having cleansed himself of all sins and accomplished all his acts
according to the best of his power and having abstained from giving pain
to any man, meets with death when it comes. The death that one meets with
by taking poison, by hanging, by burning, at the hands of robbers, and at
the teeth of animals, is said to be an inglorious one.[1555] Those men
that are righteous never incur such or similar deaths even if they be
afflicted with mental and physical diseases of the most agonising kind."

The lives of those that are sinful\nsink into the lowest depths. There is only one foe (of man) and not\nanother. That foe is identifiable with ignorance, O king. Overwhelmed by\nit, one is led to perpetrate acts that are frightful and exceedingly\ncruel. That foe for resisting which one should put forth one's power by\nwaiting upon the aged according to the duties laid down in the\nSrutis--that foe which cannot be overcome except by steady\nendeavours,--meets with destruction, O king, only when it is crushed by\nthe shafts of wisdom.[1556] The man desirous of achieving merit should at\nfirst study the Vedas and observe penances, becoming a Brahmacharin. He\nshould next, entering the domestic mode of life, perform the usual\nSacrifices. Establishing his race, he should then enter the forest,\nrestraining his senses, and desirous of winning Emancipation. One should\nnever emasculate oneself by abstaining from any enjoyment. Of all births,\nthe status of humanity is preferable even if one has to become a\nChandala. Indeed, O monarch, that order of birth (viz., humanity) is the\nforemost, since by becoming a human being one succeeds in rescuing one's\nself by meritorious acts. Men always perform righteous acts, O lord,\nguided by the authority of the Srutis, so that they may not fall away\nfrom the status of humanity. That man who, having attained to the status\nof humanity that is so difficult of attainment, indulges in malice,\ndisregards righteousness and yields himself up to desire, is certainly\nbetrayed by his desires.[1557] That man who looks upon all creatures with\neyes guided by affection, regarding them worthy of being cherished with\nloving aid, who disregards all kinds of wealth, who offers them\nconsolation, gives them food, address them in agreeable words, and who\nrejoices in their happiness and grieves in their griefs, has never to\nsuffer misery in the next world. Their bodies should be taken to the\ncrematorium on vehicles and there they should be burnt according to the\nrites of purification that have been laid down in the scriptures.\nReligious rites, beneficial ceremonies, the performance of sacrifices,\nofficiation at the sacrifices of others, gifts, the doing of other\nmeritorious acts, the performance, according to the best of one's power,\nof all that has been ordained in the case of one's deceased\nancestors,--all these one does for benefiting one's own self. The Vedas\nwith their six branches, and the other scriptures, O king, have been\ncreated for the good of him who is of stainless acts.'\"\n\n\"'Bhishma continued, \"All this was said by that high-souled sage unto the\nruler of the Videhas, O king, in days of old for his benefit.\"'\""

endure the consequences arising from it.[1560] They, however, that are of
cleansed souls and that realise the existence of Brahma, are never
afflicted by the fruits of their acts. Heedless in respect of one's
senses of knowledge and of action, one that is not conscious of one's
wicked acts, and whose heart is attached to both good and bad, becomes
afflicted with great fear. One who at all times becomes entirely freed
from attachments and who completely subjugates the passion of wrath, is
never stained by sin even if he lives in the enjoyment of worldly
objects. As a dyke built across a river, if not washed away, causes the
waters thereof to swell up, even so the man who, without being attached
to objects of enjoyments, creates the dyke of righteousness whose
materials consist of the limitations set down in the scriptures, has
never to languish. On the other hand, his merits and penances increase.

understanding is said to be dissociated from the objects of the senses.

dragged (to his ruin) by his heart which runs after all worldly objects,

constantly running towards the jaws of Death, the accomplishment of
righteous acts is proper at all times. Like a blind man who, with
attention, is capable of moving about his own house, the man of wisdom,

follow).[1563] It has been said that death arises in consequence of

course of the duties of Emancipation revolves like a wheel between birth

The\nDiverse are the fruits represented by the not-Soul. Renunciation (which\nis identical with Few) is productive of the soul's benefit.[1572] One's\nfriends who spring up from one's determination, and one's kinsmen whose\nattachment is due to (selfish) reasons, one's spouses and sons and\nservants, only devour one's wealth. Neither the mother, nor the father,\ncan confer the slightest benefit upon one in the next world. Gifts\nconstitute the diet upon which one can subsist. Indeed, one must have to\nenjoy the fruits of one's own acts.[1573] The mother, the son, the sire,\nthe brother, the wife, and friends, are like lines traced with gold by\nthe side of gold itself.[1574] All acts, good and bad, done in past lives\ncome to the doer. Knowing that everything one enjoys or endures at\npresent is the result of the acts of past lives, the soul urges the\nunderstanding on different directions (so that it may act in such a way\nas to avoid all unpleasant fruits). Relying on earnest endeavour, and\nequipped with proper aids, he who sets himself to accomplish his tasks\nnever meets with failure. As the rays of light never abandon the Sun,\neven so prosperity never abandons one who is endued with undoubting\nfaith. That act which a man of stainless soul does with faith and\nearnestness, with the aid of proper means, without pride, and with\nintelligence, becomes never lost. A creature obtains from the very time\nof his abode in the mother's womb all his own acts good and bad that were\nachieved by him in his past lives. Death, which is irresistible, aided by\nTime which brings about the destruction of life, leads all creatures to\ntheir end like wind scattering the dust of sawed timber.[1575] Through\nacts good and bad performed by himself in his past lives, man obtains\ngold and animals and spouses, and children, and honour of birth, and\npossessions of value, and his entire affluence.'\"\n\n\"'Bhishma continued, \"Thus addressed conformably to the truth by the sage,\nJanaka, that foremost of righteous persons, O king, heard everything the\nRishi said and obtained great happiness from it.\"'\""

possessed of learning should never aim them at others. If a person deeply
pierces a man of wisdom with wordy shafts, the wise man should then
adopt peace (without giving way to wrath). The man who, though sought to
be angered, rejoices without yielding to anger, taketh away from the
provoker all his merits. That man of righteous soul, who, full of joy and
freed from malice, subdues his blazing wrath which, if indulged, would
lead him to speak ill of others and verily become his foe, takes away the
merits of others. As regards myself, I never answer when another speaks
ill of me. If assailed, I always forgive the assault. The righteous are
of opinion that forgiveness and truth and sincerity and compassion are
the foremost (of all virtues). Truth is the arcanum of the Vedas. The
arcanum of Truth is self-restraint. The arcanum of self-restraint is
Emancipation. This is the teaching of all the scriptures. I regard that
person to be Brahmana and Muni who subjugates the rising impulse of
speech, the impulse of wrath appearing in the mind, the impulse of thirst
(after unworthy things), and the impulses of the stomach and the organ of
pleasure. One who does not yield to wrath is superior to one who does.

As weak fishes, O son of Kunti, fallen into the net,\nbecome entangled in it, even so, O monarch, men destitute of the\npuissance of Yoga, encounter destruction (amid the bonds of the world).\nAs birds, O chastiser of foes, when entangled in the fine nets of fowlers\n(if weak) meet with their ruin but if endued with strength effect their\nescape, after the same manner does it happen with Yogins, O chastiser of\nfoes. Bound by the bonds of action, they that are weak meet with\ndestruction, while they that are possessed of strength break through\nthem. A small and weak fire, O king, becomes extinguished when large logs\nof timber are placed upon it. Even so the Yogin that is weak, O king,\nmeets with ruin (when brought in contact with the world and its\nattachments). The same fire, however, O monarch, when it becomes strong,\nwould (without being extinguished) burn with the aid of the wind, the\nwhole Earth. After the same manner, the Yogin, when grown in strength,\nburning with energy, and possessed of might, is capable of scorching the\nentire Universe like the Sun that rises at the time of the universal\ndissolution. As a weak man, O king, is swept away by a current, even so\nis a weak Yogin helplessly carried away by objects of the senses. An\nelephant withstands a mighty current. After the same manner, a Yogin,\nhaving acquired Yoga-puissance, withstands all objects of the senses.\nIndependent of all things, Yogins, endued with Yoga-puissance and\ninvested with lordship, enter into (the hearts of) the very lords of\ncreation, the Rishis, the deities, and the great Beings in the universe.\nNeither Yama, nor the Destroyer, nor Death himself of terrible prowess,\nwhen angry, ever succeeds in prevailing over the Yogin, O king, who is\npossessed of immeasurable energy. The Yogin, acquiring Yoga-puissance,\ncan create thousands of bodies and with them wander over the earth. Some\namongst them enjoy objects of the senses and then once more set\nthemselves to the practice of the austerest penances, and once again,\nlike the Sun (withdrawing his rays), withdraw themselves from such\npenances.[1582] The Yogin, who is possessed of strength and whom bonds\nbind not, certainly succeeds in attaining to Emancipation. I have now\ndiscoursed to thee, O monarch, on all these powers of Yoga. I shall once\nmore tell thee what the subtile powers of Yoga are with their\nindications. Hear, O chief of Bharata's race, the subtile indications of\nthe Dharana and the Samadhi of the Soul (such as Yoga brings\nabout).[1583] As a bowman who is heedful and attentive succeeds in\nstriking the aim, even so the Yogin, with absorbed soul, without doubt,\nattains to Emancipation. As a man fixing his mind on a vessel full of\nsome liquid (placed on his head) heedfully ascends a flight of steps,\neven so the Yogin, fixed and absorbed in his soul, cleanses it and makes\nit as effulgent as the Sun. As a boat, O son of Kunti, that is tossed on\nthe bosom of the sea is very soon taken by a heedful boatman to the other\nshore, even so the man of knowledge by fixing his soul in Samadhi,\nattains to Emancipation, which is so difficult to acquire, after casting\noff his body, O monarch. As a heedful charioteer, O king, having yoked\ngood steeds (unto his car) takes the car-warrior to the spot he wishes,\neven so the Yogin, O monarch, heedful in Dharana, soon attains to the\nhighest spot (viz., Emancipation) like a shaft let off from the bow\nreaching the object aimed at. The Yogin who stays immovably after having\nentered his self into the soul, destroys his sins and obtains that\nindestructible spot which is the possession of those that are righteous.\nThat Yogin who, heedfully observant of high vows, properly unites, O king,\nhis Jiva-soul with the subtile Soul in the navel, the throat, the head,\nthe heart, the chest, the sides, the eye, the ear, and the nose, burns\nall his acts good and bad of even mountain-like proportions, and having\nrecourse to excellent Yoga, attains to Emancipation.\"\n\n\"'Yudhishthira said, \"It behoveth thee to tell me, O grandsire, what the\nkinds of diet are by taking which, and what the things are by conquering\nwhich, the Yogin, O Bharata, acquires Yoga-puissance.\""
}

By drinking only water mixed with milk, first only once\nduring the day, then once during a fortnight, then once during a month,\nthen once during three months, and then once during a whole year, the\nYogin acquires Yoga-puissance. By abstaining entirely from meat, O king,\nthe Yogin of cleansed soul acquires puissance.[1584] By subjugating lust,\nand wrath, and heat, and cold and rain, and fear, and grief, and the\nbreath, and all sounds that are agreeable to men, and objects of the\nsenses, and the uneasiness, so difficult to conquer, that is born of\nabstention from sexual congress, and thirst that is so terrible, O king,\nand the pleasures of touch, and sleep, and procrastination that is almost\nunconquerable, O best of kings, high-souled Yogins, divested of\nattachments, and possessed of great wisdom, aided by their\nunderstandings, and equipped with wealth of contemplation and study,\ncause the subtile soul to stand confessed in all its glory. This high\n(Yoga) path of learned Brahmanas is exceedingly difficult to tread. No\none can walk along this path with ease. That path is like a terrible\nforest which abounds with innumerable snakes and crawling vermin, with\n(concealed) pits occurring every where, without water for slaking one's\nthirst, and full of thorns, and inaccessible on that account. Indeed, the\npath of Yoga is like a road along which no edibles occur, which runs\nthrough a desert having all its trees burnt down in a conflagration, and\nwhich has been rendered unsafe by being infested with bands of robbers.\nVery few young men can pass safely through it (for reaching the goal).\nLike unto a path of this nature, few Brahmanas can tread alone the\nYoga-path with ease and comfort. That man who, having betaken himself to\nthis path, ceases to go forward (but turns back after having made some\nprogress), is regarded as guilty of many faults. Men of cleansed souls, O\nlord of Earth, can stay with ease upon Yoga-contemplation which is like\nthe sharp edge of a razor. Persons of uncleansed souls, however, cannot\nstay on it. When Yoga-contemplation becomes disturbed or otherwise\nobstructed, it can never lead the Yogin to an auspicious end even as a\nvessel that is without a captain cannot take the passengers to the other\nshore. That man, O son of Kunti, who practises Yoga-contemplation\naccording to due rites, succeeds in casting off both birth and death, and\nhappiness and sorrow. All this that I have told thee has been stated in\nthe diverse treatises bearing upon Yoga. The highest fruits of Yoga are\nseen in persons of the regenerate order. That highest fruit is\nidentification with Brahma. The high-souled Yogin, possessed of\ngreatness, can enter into and come out of, at his will, Brahma himself\nwho is the lord of all deities, and the boon-giving Vishnu, and Bhava,\nand Dharma, and the six-faced Kartikeya, and the (spiritual) sons of\nBrahmana, the quality of Darkness that is productive of much pain, and\nthat of Passion, and that of Sattwa which is pure, and Prakriti which is\nthe highest, and the goddess Siddhi who is the spouse of Varuna, and all\nkinds of energy, and all enduring patience, and the bright lord of stars\nin the firmament with the stars twinkling all around, and the Viswas, and\nthe (great) snakes, and the Pitris, and all the mountains and hills, and\nthe great and terrible oceans, and all the rivers, and the rain-charged\nclouds, and serpents, and trees, and Yakshas, and the cardinal and\nsubsidiary points of the compass, and the Gandharvas, and all male\npersons and all female ones also. This discourse, O king, that is\nconnected with the Supreme Being of mighty energy should be regarded as\nauspicious. The Yogin has Narayana for his soul. Prevailing over all\nthings (through his contemplation of the Supreme deity), the high-souled\nYogin is capable of creating all things.\"'\"\n\nThe end of the Santi Parva [, Part two of three]."

followers of the Sankhya doctrine have been established by all the great
and puissant Yatis having Kapila their first. In that doctrine O chief of
men, no errors are discoverable. Many, indeed, are its merits. In fact,
there is no fault in it. Comprehending with the aid of knowledge that all
objects exist with faults, indeed, understanding that the objects--so
difficult to cast off--with which human beings and Pisachas and Rakshasas
and Yakshas and snakes and Gandharvas and pitris and those that are
wandering in the intermediate orders of beings (such as birds and
animals) and great birds (such as Garuda and others) and the Maruts and
royal sages and regenerate sages and Asuras and Viswedevas and the
celestial Rishis and Yogins invested with supreme puissance and the
Prajapatis and Brahman himself are engaged, and understanding truly what
the highest limit is of one's period of existence in this world, and
apprehending also the great truth, O foremost of eloquent men, about what
is called felicity here, having a clear knowledge of what the sorrows are
that overtake when the hour comes all those that are concerned with
(transitory) objects and knowing full well the sorrows of those that have
fallen into the intermediate orders of being and of those that have sunk
into hell, perceiving all the merits and all the faults of heaven, O
Bharta, and all the demerits that attach to the declarations of the Vedas
and all the excellencies that are connected with them recognising the
faults and merits of the Yoga and the Sankhya systems of philosophy,
realizing also that the quality of Sattwa has ten properties, that of
Rajas has nine, and that of Tamas has eight, that the Understanding has
seven properties, the Mind has six, and Space has five, and once more
conceiving that the Understanding has four properties and Tamas has
three, and the Rajas has two and Sattwa has one, and truly apprehending
the path that is followed by all objects when destruction overtakes them
and what the course is of self knowledge, the Sankhyas, possessed of
knowledge and experience and exalted by their perceptions of causes, and
acquiring thorough auspiciousness, attain to the felicity of Emancipation
like the rays of the Sun, or the Wind taking refuge in Space.[1585]
Vision is attached to form, the sense of scent to smell, the ear to
sound, the tongue to juices, and the skin (or body) to touch. The wind
has for its refuge Space. Stupefaction has Tamas (Darkness) for its
refuge. Cupidity has the objects of the senses for its refuge. Vishnu is
attached to (the organs of) motion. Sakra is attached to (the organs of)
strength. The deity of fire is attached to the stomach, Earth is attached
to the Waters. The Waters have Heat (or fire) for their refuge. Heat
attaches itself to the Wind; and the wind has Space for its refuge; and
Space has Mahat for its refuge, and Mahat has the Understanding for its
foundation. The Understanding has its refuge in Tamas; Tamas has Rajas
for its refuge; Rajas is founded upon Sattwa; and Sattwa is attached to
the Soul. The soul has the glorious and puissant Narayana for its refuge.
That glorious deity has Emancipation for his refuge. Emancipation is
independent of all refuge. Knowing that this body, that is endued with
six and ten possessions, is the result of the quality of Sattwa,
understanding fully the nature of the physical organism and the character
of the Chetana that dwells within it, recognising the one existent Being
that lives in the body viz., the Soul, which stands aloof from every
concern of the body and in which no sin can attach, realising the nature
of that second object, viz., the acts of persons attached to the objects
of the senses, understanding also the character of the senses and the
sensual objects which have their refuge in the Soul, appreciating the
difficulty of Emancipation and the scriptures that bear upon it knowing
fully the nature of the vital breaths called Prana, Apana, Samana, Vyana,
and Udana, as also the two other breaths, viz., the one going downward
and the other moving upward, indeed, knowing those seven breaths ordained
to accomplish seven different functions, ascertaining the nature of the
Prajapatis and the Rishis and the high paths, many in number, of virtue
or righteousness, and the seven Rishis and the innumerable royal Rishis,
O scorcher of foes, and the great celestial Rishis and the other
regenerate Rishis endued with the effulgence of the Sun, beholding all
these falling away from their puissance in course of many long ages, O
monarch, hearing of the destruction of even of all the mighty beings in
the universe, understanding also the inauspicious end that is attained, O
king, by creatures of sinful acts, and the miseries endured by those that
fall into the river Vaitarani in the realms of Yama, and the inauspicious
wanderings of creatures through diverse wombs, and the character of their
residence in the unholy uterus in the midst of blood and water and phlegm
and urine and faeces, all of foul smell, and then in bodies that result
from the union of blood and the vital seed, of marrow and sinews,

Like its\nsubstantive prototype with its equine head disgorging flames of fire,\nthis ocean too has its fiery terrors. Having transcended the liability,\nthat is so difficult to transcend, of dwelling within the gross body, the\nSankhyas enter into pure space.[1589] Surya then bears, with his rays,\nthose righteous men that are practicers of the Sankhya doctrines. It behoveth thee to tell me properly what the truth is in\nrespect, O thou of Kuru's race. I do not think it proper to question any\none else than thee! Observing the scriptures bearing upon Emancipation, I\nfind this great fault in the subject (for certain scriptures on the topic\ndeclare that consciousness disappears in the emancipate state, while\nother scriptures declare the very reverse of this). If, having attained\nto this high state, the Yatis continue to live in consciousness, it would\nseem, O king, that the religion of Pravritti is superior. If, again,\nconsciousness disappears from the emancipate state and one who has become\nemancipate only resembles a person sunk in dreamless slumber, then\nnothing can be more improper than to say that there is really no\nconsciousness in Emancipation (for of all that happens in dreamless\nslumber is that one's consciousness is temporarily overshadowed and\nsuspended, but never lost, for it returns when one awakes from that\nslumber).\"[1593]\n\n\"'Bhishma said, \"However difficult it may be to answer it, the question\nwhich thou hast asked, O son, is proper. For all that, hear\nwhat the truth is as expounded by me. The high-souled followers of Kapila\nhave set their high understandings on this point. The senses of\nknowledge, O King, planted in the bodies of embodied creatures, are\nemployed in their respective functions of perception. They are the\ninstruments of the Soul, for it is through them that subtile Being\nperceives.[1594] Disunited with the Soul, the senses are like lumps of\nwood, and are without doubt, destroyed (in respect of the functions they\nserve) like the froth that is seen on the bosom of the ocean.[1595] When\nthe embodied creature, O scorcher of foes, sinks into sleep along with\nhis senses, the subtile Soul then roves among all subjects like the wind\nthrough space.[1596] The subtile Soul, during slumber, continues to see\n(all forms) and touch all objects of touch, O king, and taken in other\nperceptions, as well as when it is awake. In consequence of their\ninability to act without their director, the senses, during sleep, all\nbecome extinguished in their respective places (and lose their powers)\nlike snakes deprived of poison.[1597] At such times, the subtile Soul,\nrepairing into the respective place of all the senses, without doubt,\ndischarges all their functions.[1598] All the qualities of Sattwa, all\nthe attributes of the Understanding, O Bharata, as also those of Mind,\nand space, and Wind, O thou of righteous soul, and all the attributes of\nliquid substances, of Water, O Partha, and of Earth,--these senses with\nthese qualities,--O Yudhishthira, which inhere to Jiva-souls, are along\nwith the Jiva-soul itself, overwhelmed by the Supreme Soul or Brahma.\nActs also, good and bad, overwhelm that Jiva-soul. Like disciples waiting\nupon their preceptor with reverence, the senses too wait upon the\nJiva-soul transcends Prakriti, it attains to Brahma that is without\nchange, that is highest, that is Narayana, that is beyond all pairs of\nopposites, and that transcends Prakriti. Freed from both merit and\ndemerit, the Jiva-soul entering the Supreme Soul which is divested of all\nattributes, and which is the home of all auspiciousness, does not return\nthence, O Bharata. What remains, O son, is the mind with the senses, O\nBharata. These have to come back once more at the appointed season for\ndoing the bidding of their great master.[1599] Soon after, O son of\nKunti, (when this body is cast off) the Yati striving after Emancipation,\nendued as he is with knowledge and desirous as he is of Guna, succeeds in\nattaining to that Peace of Emancipation which is his who becomes\nbodiless.[1600] [1601] The Sankhyas, O king, are endued with great\nwisdom. They succeed in attaining to the highest end by means of this\nkind of knowledge. There is no knowledge that is equal to this. Do not\nyield to any kind of doubt. The knowledge which is described in the\nsystem of the Sankhyas is regarded as the highest. That knowledge is\nimmutable and is eternally fixed. It is eternal Brahma in fulness. It has\nno beginning, middle and end. It transcends all pairs of opposites. It is\nthe cause of the creation of the universe. It stands in fulness. It is\nwithout deterioration of any kind. It is uniform, and everlasting. Thus\nare its praises sung by the wise. From it flow creation and destruction\nand all modifications. The great Rishis speak of it and applaud it in the\nscriptures. All learned Brahmanas and all righteous men regard it as\nflowing from Brahma, Supreme, Divine, Infinite, Immutable, and\nUndeteriorating. All Brahmanas again that are attached to objects of the\nsenses adore and applaud it by ascribing to it attributes that belong to\nillusion.[1602] The same is the view of Yogins well observant of penances\nand meditation and of Sankhyas of immeasureable insight. The Srutis\ndeclare, O son of Kunti, that the Sankhya form of philosophy is the form\nof that Formless one. That high knowledge,\nO king, which exists in persons conversant with Brahma, and that which\noccurs in the Vedas, and that which is found in other scriptures, and\nthat in Yoga, and that which may be seen in the diverse Puranas, are all,\nO monarch, to be found in Sankhya philosophy.[1604] Whatever knowledge is\nseen to exist in high histories, whatever knowledge occurs, O king, in the\nsciences appertaining to the acquisition of wealth as approved by the\nwise, whatever other knowledge exists in this world,--all these,--flow, O\nhigh-souled monarch, from the high knowledge that occurs among the\nSankhyas. Those regenerate persons that are\ndevoted to the acquisition of that knowledge which is recommended in the\nSankhya system, even if they fail to attain to eminence, are never seen\nto fall among intermediate creatures, or to sink into the status of\nsinful men. That high-souled person who is fully conversant with the\nvast, high, ancient, ocean-like, and immeasurable Sankhya system that is\npure and liberal and agreeable, becomes, O king, equal to Narayana. }

Twelve thousand years, (according to the measure\nof the celestials), make a Yuga, four such Yugas taken a thousand times,\nmake a Kalpa which measures one day of Brahman.[1609] Brahman's night\nalso, O king, is of the same measure. When Brahman himself is\ndestroyed,[1610] Sambhu of formless soul and to whom the Yuga attributes\nof Anima, Laghima, &c, naturally inhere, awakes, and once more creates\nthat First or Eldest of all creatures, possessed of vast proportions, of\ninfinite deeds, endued with form, and identifiable with the universe.\nThat Sambhu is otherwise called Isana (the lord of everything). This is called by the\nlearned the Creation of Knowledge. The creation of Mahan (or Virat) and\nConsciousness, by Hiranyagarbha, is the creation of Ignorance.[1611]\nAscription of attributes (worthy of worship) and the destruction thereof,\ncalled respectively by the names of Ignorance and Knowledge by persons\nlearned by the interpretation of the Srutis, then arose, referring to\nthis, that, or the other of the three (viz., Akshara, Hiranyagarbha, or\nVirat).[1612] Know, O king, that the creation of the (subtile) elements\nfrom consciousness is the third.[1613] In all kinds of consciousness is\nthe fourth creation which flows modification of the third. Whatever other creatures exist in water or space or\non earth, for there is no other place in which creatures exist as we have\nheard, have this combination. All these, O sire, included within the\nclass called Manifest, are seen to be destroyed day after day. Hence, all\ncreatures produced by union of these four and twenty are said to be\ndestructible."
}

That Vishnu in consequence of the absence of all attributes, is\nnot a topic (of knowledge) though as then which pervades all the topics,\nhe has been called so by the wise. Since that which is destructible has\ncaused all this that is Manifest, therefore, all this is endued with\nform. The twenty-fourth, which is Prakriti, is said to preside over all\nthis (which has sprung from her modifications). The twenty-fifth, which\nis Vishnu, is formless and, therefore, cannot be said to preside over the\nuniverse.[1614] It is that Unmanifest (Prakriti), which, when endued with\nbody (in consequence of union with Chit) dwells in the hearts of all\ncreatures endued with body. As regards eternal Chetana (the\nIndestructible), although he is without attributes and without form, yet\nhe (in consequence of a union with Prakriti) assumes all forms. Uniting\nwith Prakriti which has the attributes of birth and death, he also\nassumes the attributes of birth and death. And in consequence of such\nunion he becomes an object of perception and though in reality divested\nof all attributes yet he comes to be invested therewith. It is in this\nway that the Mahan-Soul (Hiranyagarbha), becoming united with Prakriti\nand invested with Ignorance, undergoes modifications and becomes\nconscious of Self. Uniting with the attributes of Sattwa and Rajas and\nTamas, he becomes identified with diverse creatures belonging to diverse\norders of Being, in consequence of his forgetfulness and his waiting upon\nIgnorance. In consequence of his birth and destruction arising from the\nfact of his dwelling in upon with Prakriti, he thinks himself to be no\nother than what he apparently is. Regarding himself as this or that, he\nfollows the attributes of Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas. Under the influence\nof Tamas, he attains to diverse kinds of conditions that are affected by\nTamas. Under the influence of Rajas and Sattwa, he attains similarly to\nconditions that are affected by Rajas and Sattwa. There are three colours\nin all, viz., White, Red, and Dark. All those colours appertain to\nPrakriti (so that He it is who becomes White or Red or Dark according as\nthe nature of the Prakriti with which is He becomes identified for the\ntime being). Through Tamas one goes to hell. Through Rajas one attains to\nand remains in the status of humanity. Through Sattwa, people ascend to\nthe regions of the deities and become sharers of great felicity. By\nadhering to sin continuously one sinks into the intermediate order of\nbeings. By acting both righteously and sinfully one attains to the status\nof the deities. In this way the twenty-fifth, viz., Akshara (the\nIndestructible), the wise say, by union with the unmanifest (Prakriti),\nbecomes transformed into Kshara (destructible). By means of knowledge\nhowever, the Indestructible becomes displayed in His true nature.'\"'\""

afflicted by headache and opthalmia and toothache and affections of the

glands, and cholera, and vitiligo, and leprosy, and burns, and asthma and
phthisis, and epilepsy, and whatever other diseases of diverse kinds are
seen in the bodies of embodied creatures. Regarding himself, through
error, as born among thousands of creatures in the intermediate orders of
being, and sometimes among the gods, he endures misery and enjoys the
fruits of his good deeds. Invested with Ignorance he regards himself as
robed sometimes in white cloth and sometimes in full dress consisting of
four pieces or as lying on floors (instead of on beds or bedsteads) or
with hands and feet contracted like those of frogs or as seated upright
in the attitude of ascetic contemplation, or as clad in rags or as lying

in fabric of hemp, or in barks of birch or in cloths made of the produce

soul regards himself also as wearing diverse kinds of ornaments and gems,
or as eating diverse kinds of food. He regards himself as sometimes
eating at intervals of one night, or once at the same hour every day, or
as at the fourth, the sixth, and the eighth hour every day, or as once in
six or seven or eight nights, or as once in ten or twelve day, or as once
in a month, of as eating only roots, or fruits, or as subsisting upon air
or water alone, or on cakes of sesame husk, or curds or cowdung, or the
urine of the cow or potherbs or flowers or moss or raw food, or as
subsisting on fallen leaves of trees or fruits that have fallen down and
lay scattered on the ground, or diverse other kinds of food, impelled by
the desire of winning (ascetic) success. The Soul regards himself as
adopting the observance of Chandrayana according to the rites ordained in
the scriptures, or diverse other vows and observance, and the courses of
duty prescribed for the four modes of life, and even derelictions of
duty, and the duties of other subsidiary modes of life included in the
four principal ones, and even diverse kinds of practices that distinguish
the wicked and sinful. The Soul regards himself as enjoying retired spots
and delightful shades of mountains and the cool vicinity of spring and
fountain and solitary river banks and secluded forests, and sacred spots
dedicated to the deities, and lakes and waters withdrawn from the busy
hunts of men, and lone mountain caves affording the accommodation that
houses and mansions afford. The Soul regards himself as employed in the
recitation of different kinds of hidden Mantras or as observing different
vows and rules and diverse kinds of penances, and sacrifices of many
kinds, and rites of diverse sorts. The Soul regards himself as adopting
sometimes the way of traders and merchants and the practices of Brahmanas
and Kshatriyas and Vaisyas and Sudras, and gifts of diverse kinds unto
those that are destitute or blind or helpless. In consequence of his
being invested with Ignorance, the Soul adopts different attributes of
Sattwa and Rajas and Tamas, and Righteousness and Wealth and pleasure.

as such. Indeed, the Soul regards himself as employed in the utterance of

invested with all these conditions, which are his own forms and
attributes, infinite in number, and agreeable to himself. It is this way"

O monarch, the whole of this universe has\nbeen blinded by Prakriti and all things have been diversely overwhelmed\n(through Prakriti) by the attributes of Rajas and Tamas. It is in\nconsequence of the Soul being invested by Prakriti that these pairs of\nopposites productive of happiness and woe, repeatedly come. It is in\nconsequence of this Ignorance that Jiva regards these sorrows to be his\nand imagines them as pursuing him. Indeed, O monarch, through that\nIgnorance it is that Jiva imagines he should anyhow cross those sorrows,\nand that he should, going into the regions of the gods, enjoy the\nfelicity that awaits all his good acts. It is through Ignorance that he\nthinks he should enjoy and endure these delights and these woes here in\nthis world. Through Ignorance Jiva thinks,--\"I should secure my happiness.\nBy continually doing good acts, I may have happiness in this life till\nits close and I shall be happy in all my future lives. Though, again the\n(evil) acts I do in this life unending sorrow may become mine. The status\nof humanity is fraught with great misery, for from it one sinks into\nhell. From that superior status I shall have to come back again to\nhumanity and thence to sink into hell once more!\"--One who always regards\nthis combination of the primal elements and the senses, with the Chit's\nreflection in it, to be thus invested with the characteristics of the\nSoul, has repeatedly to wander among gods and human beings and to sink\ninto hell. Being always invested with the idea of meum, Jiva has to make\na round of such births. Millions upon millions of births have to be gone\nthrough by Jiva in the successive forms he assumes, all of which are\nliable to death. He who does acts in this way, which are all fraught with\ngood and bad fruits, has in the three worlds to assume successive forms\nand to enjoy and endure fruits corresponding therewith. It is Prakriti\nthat causes acts fraught with good and bad acts; and it is Prakriti that\nenjoys and endures the fruits thereof in the three worlds. Indeed,\nPrakriti follows the course of acts. The status of the intermediate\nbeings, of humanity, and of the gods as well,--these three\nfields,--should be known as originating in Prakriti and has been said to\nbe destitute of all attributes. Her existence is affirmed only in\nconsequence of her acts (beginning with Mahat). After the same manner,\nPurusha (or Soul), though without attributes himself, has his existence\naffirmed in consequence of the acts which the body does when it receives\nhis reflection. Although the Soul is not subject to modifications of any\nkind and is the active principle that sets Prakriti in motion, yet\nentering a body that is united with the senses of knowledge and action,\nhe regards all the acts of those senses as his own. The five senses of\nknowledge beginning with the ear, and those of action beginning with\nspeech, uniting with the attributes of Sattwa and Rajas and Tamas, become\nengaged in numerous objects. Jiva imagines that it is he who does the acts\nof his life and that the senses of knowledge and acts belong to him,\nalthough in reality he has no senses. Indeed, though unequipt with body,\nhe imagines that he has a body. Though destitute of attributes, he\nregards himself as endued therewith, and though transcending Time,\nimagines himself to be under Time's control. Though destitute of\nunderstanding, he still regards himself as endued therewith, and though\ntranscending the (four and twenty) topics, regards himself as one\nincluded among them. Though deathless, he still regards himself as liable\nto death, and though motionless regards himself to be endued with motion.\nThough not possessed of a material case, he still regards himself as\npossessed of one; and though unborn, he still regards himself as\ninvested with birth. Though transcending penances, he still regards as\nengaged in penances, and though he has no end (after which to strive), he\nstill regards himself as liable to attain to ends (of diverse kinds).\nThough not endued with motion and birth, he still regards himself as\nendued with both, and though transcending fear, still regards himself as\nliable to fear. Though Indestructible, he still regards himself\nDestructible. Invested with Ignorance, the Soul thus thinks of himself.'\"'\""

With the\neternal and immutable portion on Jiva primal essence become united and\nthis union takes place repeatedly. That sixteenth portion is subtile. Since those\nsixteen portions are the cause of the birth of creatures, creatures can\nnever, O monarch, take birth without their aid. They are called Prakriti.\nThe destruction of Jiva's liability to be united with Prakriti is called\nEmancipation. The Mahat-Soul, which is the twenty-fifth, if it regards\nthat body of sixteen portions called the Unmanifest,[1617] has to assume\nit repeatedly. In consequence of not knowing, That which is stainless and\npure, and for its devotion to what is the result of a combination of both\nPure and Impure, the Soul, which is in reality pure, becomes, O king\nImpure. Indeed, in consequence of its devotion to Ignorance, Jiva, though\ncharacterised by Knowledge becomes repeatedly associated with Ignorance.\nThough, O monarch, free from error of every kind, yet in consequence of\nits devotion to the three attributes of Prakriti, it becomes endued with\nthose attributes.'\"'\""

however, in thy understanding, only the texts of the Vedas and the other
scriptures. Thou art not, O monarch, truly conversant with the real
meaning of those texts. That person who bears in his understanding merely
the texts of the Vedas and the other scriptures without being conversant
with the true sense or meaning of those texts, bears them fruitlessly.
Indeed, one who holds the contents of a work in memory without
comprehending their meaning is said to bear an useless burden. He,
however, who is conversant with the true meaning of a treatise, is said
to have studied that treatise to purpose. Questioned regarding the
meaning of a text, it behoveth one to communicate that meaning which he
has comprehended by a careful study. That person of dull intelligence who
refuses to expound the meanings of texts in the midst of a conclave of
the learned, that person of foolish understanding, never succeeds in
expounding the meaning correctly.[1618] An ignorant person, going to
expound the true meaning of treatises, incurs ridicule. Even those
possessed of a knowledge of the Soul have to incur ridicule on such
occasions (if what they go to explain has not been acquired by study).
Listen now to me, O monarch, as to how the subject of Emancipation has
been explained (by preceptors to disciple from days of old) among
highsouled persons conversant with the Sankhya and the Yoga systems of
philosophy. That which the Yogins behold is precisely that which the
Sankhyas strive after to attain. He who sees the Sankhya and the Yoga
systems to be one and the same is said to be endued with intelligence.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, and sinews, and these senses (of
both knowledge and action), about which thou wert speaking unto me,
exist. Objects flow from objects; the senses from the senses. From body
one obtains a body, as a seed is obtained from seed. When the Supreme
Being is without senses, without seed, without matter, without body, He
must be divested of all attributes, and in consequence of His being so,
how, indeed, can He have attributes of any kind? Space and other
attributes arise from the attributes of Sattwa and Rajas and Tamas, and
disappear ultimately in them. Thus the attributes arise from Prakriti.

that are made of Prakriti, know, O king, may sometimes be produced by the
vital seed alone (of the male). The Jiva-soul and the universe are said
to both partake of Prakriti characterised by the three attributes of
Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas. The Supreme Soul is different from both the
Jiva-soul and the universe. As the seasons though unendued with forms,
are nevertheless inferred from the appearance of particular fruits and
flowers, after the same manner, Prakriti, though formless, is inferred
from the attributes of Mahat and the rest that spring from it. In this
way from the existence of Chaitanya in the body, the Supreme Soul,
divested of all attributes whatever and perfectly stainless, is inferred.

things, and auspicious, that Soul, only in consequence of its identifying
itself with the body and other attributes, comes to be taken as invested
with attributes. Those persons that are truly conversant with attributes
know that only objects endued with attributes can have attributes but
that That which transcends all attributes can have none. When the
Jiva-soul conquers all attributes born of Prakriti and which it assumes
under error, only then does it behold the Supreme Soul. Only the highest
Rishis conversant with the Sankhya and the Yoga systems know that Supreme
Soul which Sankhya and Yogins and believers in all other systems say is
beyond the Understanding, which is regarded as Knower and endued with the
highest wisdom in consequence of its casting off all consciousness of
identification with Prakriti, which transcends the attribute of Ignorance
or Error, which is Unmanifest, which is beyond all attributes, which is
called the Supreme, which is dissociated from all attributes, which
ordains all things, which is Eternal and Immutable, which overrules
Prakriti and all the attributes born of Prakriti, and which, transcending
the four and twenty topics of enquiry, forms the twenty-fifth. When men
of knowledge, who stand in fear of birth, of the several conditions of
living consciousness, and of death, succeed in knowing the Unmanifest,
they succeed in understanding the Supreme Soul at the same time. An
intelligent man regards the unity of Jiva-soul with the Supreme Soul as
consistent with the scriptures and as perfectly correct, while the man
destitute of intelligence looks upon the two as different from each
other. This forms the distinction between the man of intelligence and man
that is destitute of it. The indications of both Kshara and Akshara
(destructible and indestructible) have now been said unto thee. Akshara
is Oneness or Unity, while multiplicity or variety is said to be Kshara.
When one begins to study and understands properly the five and twenty
topics of enquiry, one then comprehends that the Oneness of the Soul is
consistent with the scriptures and its multiplicity is what is opposed to
them. These are the several indications of what is included in the tale
of topics or principles created and what transcends that tale. The wise
have said that the tale of topics numbers only five and twenty. That
which transcends the topics is beyond that number and forms the
twenty-sixth. The study or comprehension of created things (numbered five
and twenty) according to their aggregates (of five) is the study and
comprehension of topics. Transcending these is That which is eternal.'"'""
